0. Study & method

21 participants each played two games (order rotated) and were then given up to 10 minutes per game to find that game's name using whatever search strategy they liked. Screen activity was annotated by human coders into a controlled 8-value action vocabulary: Query, View result list, View single result, Platform switch, View AI response, View info box, Browsing, and Experiment ended (a per-task end marker, not a search action). 4 annotators coded the sessions. Two columns added later (action_details_clean, action_details_num_tokens — destination platform/source site and query/text length; see §7) enrich Query, Platform switch, and View single result rows specifically.

Data cleaning applied: the duplicate Experiment ended marker previously flagged for ID12 was fixed by the annotator at the source. An earlier data refresh (the one that added the two new columns) had introduced an Excel #REF! error in ID12's rank column for 3 rows — also now fixed at the source (analysis/data.py still carries a fallback repair for any future recurrence, see docs/planning_and_background.md §4.7). ID1 and ID20's added events are confirmed genuine re-annotation corrections. ID3's Best Buds session gained 4 further Platform switch events in a later annotation pass. This is now the final, stable dataset: 1,302 events across 21 participants × 2 games, and every table below reflects it — no further data-refresh caveats.

1. RQ1 — How common are the actions individually?

1.1 Overall frequency

Action Count Share
View result list 359 27.6%
Query 326 25.0%
Platform switch 240 18.4%
View single result 158 12.1%
View AI response 81 6.2%
View info box 52 4.0%
Browsing 44 3.4%
Experiment ended 42 3.2%

Query and View result list dominate, as expected for search tasks. Platform switch is the third most common action overall (18%) — notably frequent for a "find one thing" task, suggesting participants often check more than one store/platform rather than committing to a single search surface.

1.2 By game

Action Best Buds vs Bad Guys Townscaper
View result list 28.7% 24.7%
Query 26.1% 22.2%
Platform switch 18.7% 17.7%
View single result 10.2% 17.2%
View AI response 6.7% 5.0%
View info box 4.4% 3.0%
Browsing 3.0% 4.4%
Experiment ended 2.2% 5.8%

The action mix is broadly similar, but View single result is proportionally much more common in Townscaper (17% vs. 10%) — consistent with Townscaper being the task participants actually solved: they land on one correct result and stop, rather than continuing to cycle through result lists.

1.3 Session length by game

Search-only event counts per participant (excludes Experiment ended):

Game Mean Median Min Max
Best Buds vs Bad Guys 43.8 47 13 71
Townscaper 16.2 13 4 55

Success split: 20 of 21 participants found Townscaper (usually quickly); 0 of 21 found Best Buds vs Bad Guys within the 10-minute cap. The volume and length difference above isn't just "Best Buds is harder" — every Best Buds session is a search that ran out the clock unresolved, while Townscaper sessions are (almost all) resolved searches, often in very few steps. This reframes RQ3: the comparison isn't between two similarly-solved tasks, but between a resolved-search regime and a uniformly unresolved-search regime. (One Townscaper outlier ran to 55 events despite the task usually being solved fast — worth a closer look when we get to per-participant analysis.)

2. RQ2 — Typical action patterns or sequences?

Data fix found along the way: building the transition matrix assumes Experiment ended is a true absorbing end-state (no actions after it). One session (ID10, Townscaper) had a Platform switch recorded after Experiment ended — likely a stray post-task event. analysis/data.py now truncates anything after the end marker per (participant, game), dropping 1 event from the pipeline (the 1,302-event total in §0 already reflects this). See docs/planning_and_background.md §6.

2.1 The core search loop

First-order transition probabilities (results/rq2_patterns/transitions_probs_overall.csv), visualized in results/rq2_patterns/transition_graph_overall.png:

From → Most likely next action(s)
Query View result list (60%)
View result list Query (30%) · View single result (29%) · Platform switch (24%)
Platform switch Query (55%) · View result list (35%)
View AI response Query (42%)
Experiment ended (none — confirmed absorbing)

The backbone is a tight loop: Query → View result list, which then splits three ways (reformulate, drill into a result, or switch platform). Platform switch and View AI response both function as detours back into the loop rather than endpoints — over half of platform switches and 40%+ of AI-response views are immediately followed by another Query.

Top overall bigrams (results/rq2_patterns/top_2-grams_overall.csv): Query → View result list (196), Platform switch → Query (131), View result list → Query (109), View result list → View single result (105).

2.2 What "typical" looks like per game

The clearest signal is in the exit probabilities — how likely each action is to be followed by Experiment ended:

From → Experiment ended Best Buds vs Bad Guys Townscaper
View info box 4.9% 36.4%
View single result 4.2% 19.4%
View AI response 6.3% 11.1%
(all other actions) ≤3.6% ≤3.4%

Best Buds has no strong exit path at all — every action's probability of ending the session is small, consistent with 0/21 sessions resolving.

Townscaper has two clear "closing moves": viewing the info box or re-viewing a single result is, more often than not on the Townscaper side, how a session actually ends. Townscaper's top-5 trigrams (results/rq2_patterns/top_3-grams_townscaper.csv) include View single result → View single result → View single result (12 occurrences) — a repeat-to-confirm pattern that doesn't appear in Best Buds' top trigrams at all. This is a first concrete answer to RQ3, developed further there.

Interactive first-6-step flow diagrams (Sankey) and the full bigram/trigram/PrefixSpan pattern tables are in results/rq2_patterns/ — not embedded here since they're interactive Plotly pages.

3. RQ3 — How do search strategies differ between the two games?

This formalizes the resolved-vs-unresolved contrast previewed in §2.2. Full outputs in results/rq3_game_differences/.

3.1 The transition matrices really are different — but only in specific places

A chi-square test compared each action's outgoing-transition distribution between the two games (results/rq3_game_differences/transition_matrix_comparison.csv); Jensen–Shannon divergence gives a comparable effect-size that doesn't depend on chi-square's sparse-cell assumptions:

From χ² p JS divergence
View info box 20.27 0.003 0.669
View single result 24.86 <0.001 0.346
View AI response 10.21 0.116 0.372
Browsing 7.72 0.172 0.432
View result list 7.18 0.411 0.163
Query 6.38 0.496 0.132
Platform switch 3.54 0.617 0.145

Only two states show a statistically robust difference (both survive a Bonferroni correction across the 7 tests, α=0.0071): View info box and View single result — exactly the two "closing move" states identified in §2.2. The core loop (Query, View result list, Platform switch) behaves statistically the same in both games; the games diverge specifically in what happens once a participant is looking closely at a result. Pooling the full matrices gives a global JS divergence of 0.27 (0=identical, 1=disjoint) — a real but partial difference, consistent with a shared backbone plus a different ending.

3.2 Session-level features (paired by participant, n=21)

Feature Median (Best Buds) Median (Townscaper) Wilcoxon p
Session length 47 13 0.0003
Action entropy 2.16 bits 2.08 bits 0.050
Query rate 0.28 0.25 0.243
Platform-switch rate 0.19 0.20 0.338

Length aside (expected — Best Buds runs the full clock, see §1.3), query rate and platform-switch rate don't differ between games: participants query and switch platforms at similar rates regardless of whether they're going to succeed. Entropy trends slightly higher for Best Buds, not lower — the opposite of a naive "unresolved search looks more repetitive" prediction. That's addressed directly in §3.3.

3.3 Inside an unresolved search: does Best Buds plateau or keep exploring?

Splitting each Best Buds session at its midpoint and comparing halves:

  • Entropy rises, not falls, from the first half (2.06 bits) to the second half (2.23 bits), Wilcoxon p=0.042 — participants broaden their action mix as the session goes on, rather than narrowing into a tight loop.
  • But only 36% of second-half bigrams are genuinely new (not seen in the first half) — most of what happens later in the session is a repeat of bigrams already tried earlier.

Together these paint a specific picture of what a failed search looks like here: not a participant stuck repeating one or two actions (that would show falling entropy), and not a systematic widening search either (that would show a higher novel-bigram rate). It's closer to cycling through an already-explored repertoire while occasionally trying one more action type (e.g. finally opening View info box or Browsing late in the session) — broadening the action mix slightly without making much headway on genuinely new combinations.

4. RQ4 — Are there clusters of users with similar search processes?

Run separately per game (21 sessions each — pooling both games would mostly just rediscover the RQ3 resolved/unresolved split rather than within-game strategy variation). Two independent views per game, plus a leave-one-out (LOO) stability check and a cross-game consistency check. Full outputs in results/rq4_clustering/.

Method: (1) sequence-distance — normalized Levenshtein edit distance between raw action sequences, agglomerative clustering, k chosen by silhouette score; (2) feature-based — per-session action-mix vector (7 action proportions + entropy), standardized, k-means, k chosen the same way. Stability: recluster with each session left out in turn and compare (Adjusted Rand Index, ARI) against the full clustering restricted to the remaining sessions — low mean ARI would mean the clusters aren't robust to exactly which 21 people happened to be sampled.

4.1 Best Buds vs Bad Guys — two clusters, cleanly separated by AI/info-box reliance

Cluster n Query View result list View AI response View info box Entropy Length
0 — "list-browsers" 14 26% 35% 3% 1% 2.12 50
1 — "AI-assisted" 7 29% 14% 20% 12% 2.33 32

Feature-based k=2, silhouette 0.28, LOO mean ARI = 1.00 (perfectly stable across all 21 leave-one-out folds). One subgroup (n=14) searches by repeatedly opening result lists; the other (n=7) leans heavily on View AI response and View info box instead, with shorter, higher-entropy sessions. The sequence-distance view (LOO ARI also 1.00) finds a different split — 2 extreme-length outliers vs. everyone else — so the two views agree only weakly with each other (ARI 0.20): they're picking up genuinely different structure (raw session length/shape vs. action-type mix), not duplicating the same signal.

4.2 Townscaper — a small "AI-quick" subgroup stands out

Cluster n Query View AI response Browsing Length
0 — typical 17 24% 2% 4% 18
1 — "AI-quick" 4 31% 28% 0% 7

Feature-based k=2, LOO mean ARI = 0.84 (moderate-to-good — less stable than Best Buds, expected given Townscaper sessions are much shorter and more homogeneous, so there's less signal per session). The sequence-distance view again finds a different 2-way split here (LOO ARI 0.67), and the two views barely agree (ARI ≈ 0.03). With the "AI-quick" cluster this small (n=4), treat it as a descriptive lead, not a confirmed subtype. (Updated 2026-08-19: after a data correction — see §0 — the optimal k for this split shifted from 3 to 2. A small "wanderers" outlier pair, previously its own cluster, no longer separates from the majority group at the silhouette-optimal k; the "AI-quick" cluster is unchanged. Small-N clustering being this sensitive to a handful of events is itself informative — it's why §4's clusters were treated as descriptive leads throughout, not confirmed subtypes.)

4.3 Cross-game consistency: is this a personal style, or purely task-driven?

Comparing each participant's feature-based cluster label in Best Buds against their label in Townscaper gives ARI = 0.47 — a real, moderate relationship, not zero. Concretely: all 4 members of Townscaper's "AI-quick" cluster come from Best Buds' "AI-assisted" cluster (the n=7 group). So the AI/info-box-reliance dimension found in Best Buds isn't just noise from a long, unresolved task — a subset of the same people show the same tendency on Townscaper too, where it manifests as unusually fast, AI-driven resolution. That's suggestive of a genuine individual search-style difference layered on top of the game-level (RQ3) effect, though with only 4–7 people involved, this wants a larger sample before leaning on it too hard. §6's platform data (RQ7) makes this concrete: this cluster's platform switches actually go to AI assistants, and its queries are markedly longer — not just an artifact of the action-type proportions used to build the cluster.

5. RQ5 — Does the annotator influence how a search process is coded?

Two parts. 6.1–6.2 are the primary analysis: the dedicated agreement sample (data/agreement/) — participant ID13, both games, independently segmented and labeled by six annotators (annotator1–6; annotator5/6 were added 2026-09-07, expanded from an original four). annotator4 is the annotator who coded ID13 in the main dataset, so it doubles as the reference sequence. This is the only place multiple annotators coded the same recording, so it's the only place an annotator effect is actually identifiable. 6.3 is a secondary, confounded check on the 21 individually-annotated participants, added at the researcher's request — read its caveats before its numbers. Full outputs in results/rq5_annotator_agreement/ and results/rq5b_annotator_confound/.

Method note — this couldn't be a plain Cohen's kappa. The six annotators' files have different row counts — they independently segmented the recording, not just labeled a shared fixed set of events. So there's no common "item" to rate until the sequences are aligned. Method: (1) align annotators 1–3, 5, 6 against the annotator4 reference via minimum-edit-distance sequence alignment; (2) Krippendorff's alpha (nominal) on the aligned matrix; (3) pairwise alignment-free sequence similarity (all 15 pairs) as a complementary view; (4) a pooled confusion table and per-action count comparison.

5.1 Labels agree almost perfectly — when annotators agree an event happened at all

Game Krippendorff's α (aligned)
Best Buds vs Bad Guys 0.97
Townscaper 0.91

Taken alone, these look excellent. But α only scores positions where annotators aligned to the same event — it treats an unmatched ("missing") position as simply absent data, not disagreement. That hides the real story:

Annotator Best Buds coverage Best Buds agreement-when-covered Townscaper coverage Townscaper agreement-when-covered
annotator1 94% 94% 78% 94%
annotator2 77% 100% 42% 100%
annotator3 100% 100% 82% 92%
annotator5 82% 100% 56% 88%
annotator6 82% 100% 56% 96%

Coverage = share of the reference annotator's (annotator4's) events that this annotator also identified at all. When annotators do align on the same event, they almost always label it identically (88–100%) — the labeling scheme itself isn't the problem. The problem is segmentation, and it's not just one outlier: annotator2 is the extreme case (42% Townscaper coverage), but annotator5/annotator6 sit in a moderate band below annotator1/annotator3 (56% vs. 78–82%) — coding granularity looks more like a spectrum than a single bad apple, worse for the longer, more repetitive Townscaper sessions across the board. annotator5 and annotator6 are, however, nearly identical to each other (similarity 1.00 on Best Buds, 0.81 on Townscaper).

5.2 Practical implication for the main dataset

In the main 21-participant dataset, annotator2 coded ID6–ID10 (§1). If annotator2's coarser segmentation style shown above generalizes, those 5 participants' session lengths/action counts in RQ1–RQ4 are likely undercounts relative to how the other annotators would have coded the same recordings — a real, if modest (5/21 participants), source of noise layered on top of the genuine between-participant variation those analyses report. §5.3 checks this directly.

5.3 Secondary check on the main dataset — confounded, read the caveat first

Every result in this subsection compares blocks of participants, not annotators in isolation: annotator1→ID1–5, annotator2→ID6–10, annotator4→ID11–15, annotator3→ID16–21. Annotator and "which five/six participants" are the same partition of the data, so anything found here could be genuine annotator style, or it could just be that those particular people behave differently — this dataset alone cannot tell the two apart. Treat everything below as descriptive, cross-checked against 6.1's unconfounded finding where possible, not as independent proof of an annotator effect. Every feature is computed per (participant, game) first and normalized within that session before averaging within an annotator's block, so one long session can't dominate its annotator's average.

The corroboration is real but partial. Comparing annotator2's profile against the other three's average:

Action annotator2 other annotators difference
View result list 22.1% 26.1% −4.0pp
View single result 10.5% 15.0% −4.5pp
Platform switch 17.0% 20.0% −3.0pp
Browsing 2.4% 3.0% −0.6pp
View AI response 12.2% 6.9% +5.3pp
View info box 8.0% 3.3% +4.7pp

The three actions RQ5's agreement sample flagged as undercounted (View result list, Platform switch, and — closely related — View single result) are all lower for annotator2's block here too, consistent with the coarser-segmentation finding. But View AI response and View info box are higher, not lower — the opposite of a simple "undercounts everything" story. The likely mechanism: if annotator2 tends to merge or miss quick, routine actions (successive result-list glances) while reliably catching the more salient, memorable ones (opening an AI response or info panel), the proportion going to those salient actions would mechanically inflate even without any real behavioral difference — segmentation coarseness distorting a rate measure, not a labeling error (6.1 already showed labels are correct 88%+ of the time on aligned events). This is a plausible mechanism, not a demonstrated one.

Where the confound bites, not just caveats it: annotator2's block has the longest recorded Townscaper sessions of any annotator (mean 23.2 events vs. 10.6–16.2 for the others) — the opposite direction from what "coarser segmenter" would predict on its own. Read at face value this looks like it contradicts 6.1; more likely it just reflects that ID6–10 happened to be a slower-searching group in Townscaper, a genuine participant effect swamping any segmentation-style signal in this particular measure. That's the confound doing exactly what the plan said it would do, not a new finding.

A random-intercept model (annotator as the grouping factor, game as a fixed effect) gives the intraclass correlation — how much of the between-session variance in each action's rate sits "within annotator block" — as a summary of how much clustering-by-block exists at all, independent of cause:

Feature ICC (annotator block)
View info box 0.13
View AI response 0.13
View single result 0.06
Query 0.00
View result list 0.00
Platform switch 0.00
Browsing 0.00

(entropy is omitted — its model hits a boundary solution and doesn't converge; treat its near-zero point estimate as "no detectable block clustering," not a precise number.) Every ICC is low. Most of the variation in how a session looks is between individual people, not between annotator blocks — reassuring for RQ1–RQ4's between-participant comparisons generally. View AI response and View info box cluster the most (13% each), which lines up with the same two actions standing out in the corroboration check above.

Checked directly, because those two actions matter a lot to RQ4: does the RQ4 "AI-assisted"/"AI-quick" cluster just track annotator block, given the AI-related actions cluster the most here? No — crosstabbing cluster membership against annotator: Best Buds is close to uniform (1/2/2/2 "AI-assisted" members across the four annotators); Townscaper is 0/2/1/1 (annotator1's block has none, small enough to be chance at n=5). The cluster cuts across annotator blocks rather than tracking one of them, which is a real (if partial) reassurance that RQ4's individual-style finding isn't primarily an annotator artifact.

Bigram rates (results/rq5b_annotator_confound/annotator_bigram_profiles.csv) show the same broad pattern as the single-action rates — annotator2/annotator4 lean toward Query → View AI response-adjacent patterns more than annotator1/annotator3 — but with only 4 block-level rows to compare, this is offered as raw data for inspection rather than a further claim.

6. RQ6 — Does game order affect strategy, and do people carry a strategy over? (added at researcher's request)

Motivating idea: participants who played Townscaper first started on a successful note; participants who played Best Buds first may have built up frustration before Townscaper. Related: do people open each game the same way regardless of order, or does the second game's opening echo the first? Order (11 played Townscaper first, 10 played Best Buds first) is derived directly from the data — rank is one counter spanning both games per participant. Full outputs in results/rq6_order_effects/.

6.1 No detectable order effect on session-level features

Splitting each game's 21 sessions by whether it was played first or second and comparing length/entropy/query-rate/platform-switch-rate (Mann-Whitney U, unpaired): no feature reaches significance in either game (all p ≥ 0.24, most ≥ 0.5). Playing Best Buds after already having searched once (win or lose) doesn't measurably change how much someone queries, switches platforms, or how long they take. The frustration/ positive-note hypothesis isn't supported at the level of these aggregate session features.

6.2 But the opening move does carry over — and more so after Best Buds

Representing each session's opening as its first 3 actions and comparing each participant's own first-game-opening to their second-game-opening against a permutation-test null (10,000 random re-pairings of participants' openings):

  • Observed mean own-pair distance: 0.254, vs. 0.330 for randomly paired participants — participants are more self-consistent than chance, one-tailed permutation p = 0.029. (The null already absorbs the fact that almost everyone opens with Platform switch → Query — it's built from the same real openings, just re-paired — so this is a real above-baseline signal, not an artifact of a universal starting move.)
  • Splitting by which game came first is where it gets interesting: participants who played Best Buds first show near-perfect carryover (median own-pair distance = 0.000 — 7 of 10 have an exactly identical 3-action opening in both games) vs. Townscaper-first participants (median 0.333, only 3 of 11 exact matches). Mann-Whitney p = 0.077 — marginal at n=10/11, not a firm result, but a clear directional pattern: starting with the harder, unresolved game seems to lock in a strategy that gets repeated verbatim on the second game, more than starting with the easy win does.

This is the opposite framing from the original hypothesis but a coherent story: it's not that Best-Buds-first participants search differently in Townscaper (§6.1 found no feature differences) — it's that they open Townscaper the same way they opened Best Buds, more rigidly than Townscaper-first participants replicate their Townscaper opening in Best Buds. Ties back to RQ4's cross-game consistency finding (§4.3, ARI=0.47): this gives that consistency a direction and a plausible driver (which game came first), though both findings share the same small-n caveat.

6.3 Order doesn't predict RQ4 cluster membership

Crosstabbing play position against each game's RQ4 feature-cluster label (both now a clean 2×2, since RQ4's Townscaper split simplified to 2 clusters — see §4.2): no relationship in either game. Best Buds: Fisher exact p=1.0. Townscaper: 3 of the 4 "AI-quick" cluster members played Townscaper first (vs. 1 second), Fisher exact p=0.59 — a numerical lean opposite to what §6.2 might predict, but not close to significant with n=4 in that cluster.

6.4 RQ6.4 — Does order change how people search within each game?

§6.1 found no order effect on four summary features. This applies RQ3's full toolkit — action mix, transition matrices, closing moves, first/second-half dynamics — split by order instead of by game, to ask the sharper version of the researcher's question directly: is Best Buds searched differently after a Townscaper win, and is Townscaper searched differently after Best Buds frustration? Full outputs in results/rq6_4_order_within_game/.

Aggregate action mix: still no order effect in either game (Best Buds χ²=9.51, p=0.15; Townscaper χ²=4.13, p=0.66) — confirms §6.1 at the level of the full action-count table, not just 4 derived features.

But two specific, well-supported effects show up underneath that:

  • Townscaper: after viewing a single result, order changes what happens next — robustly (χ²=22.56, p=0.001, survives Bonferroni across the 7 from-states, α=0.0071; strengthens to p=0.0004 after stripping the opening 3 actions, so it isn't an artifact of the carried-over opening move). Concretely:
From View single result → Played first Played second (after Best Buds)
Experiment ended 25% 15%
Platform switch 29% 15%
Browsing 14% 0%
View single result (self-loop) 4% 47%

Townscaper-first participants who check a single result branch out — switch platform, browse, or confidently end the session. Participants who reach Townscaper after Best Buds instead re-check the same result again and again (a 47% self-loop, vs. 4%) rather than branching out or concluding. Reads as hesitancy/double-checking carried over from an experience where the obvious-looking result kept being wrong.

  • Best Buds: the "entropy rises through the session" finding from §3.3 is really a played-second effect. Splitting that half-split analysis further by order:
Best Buds order First-half entropy Second-half entropy Wilcoxon p Novel-bigram rate (2nd half)
Played first (n=10) 2.16 2.25 0.625 28%
Played second, after Townscaper win (n=11) 1.96 2.22 0.032 44%

When Best Buds is a participant's first task, there's no significant broadening and few genuinely new bigrams late in the session — closer to settling into repetition. When Best Buds comes after an already-won Townscaper, the entropy rise is significant and nearly half of late bigrams are genuinely new combinations — participants explore more persistently when they hit a wall, if they've already banked a win. That's the "positive note" hypothesis showing up — not in whether Best Buds gets solved (nobody solves it), but in how hard and how broadly people keep trying.

Caveat carried over from the plan: both effects are per-cell comparisons of ~10 vs. ~11 sessions, on top of an already-small study — treat as suggestive rather than confirmatory, though the Townscaper result clears the same Bonferroni bar used for the game-level comparison in RQ3 and gets stronger, not weaker, once the opening-carryover confound is controlled for.

One more data point, not a finding: the one Townscaper session that looks unresolved (55 events, far beyond the next-longest at 44 — inferred from session length, not a ground-truth outcome label) belongs to ID9, who played Best Buds first. Consistent with, though certainly not proof of, the frustration-carryover story — n=1.

7. RQ7 — Enriching the analyses with destination and query-length data

Two new columns (added by the researcher, 2026-08-19): action_details_clean (destination platform for Platform switch; source site for View single result) and action_details_num_tokens (length of the withheld free-text field — most meaningful for Query). Full outputs in results/rq7_platform_details/; method and the #REF! data-quality fix in docs/planning_and_background.md §4.7.

7.1 Platform-switch destinations ground-truth the RQ4 cluster names

Categorizing the 23 observed destinations (search engine / AI assistant / storefront / community / game database — see results/rq7_platform_details/platform_category_by_game.csv): search engines dominate both games (~78% of switches), with AI assistants slightly more common in Best Buds (10%) than Townscaper (6%), and community sites (mostly Reddit, including the aptly-named r/tipofmyjoystick) more common in Townscaper (6%) than Best Buds (2%).

The sharper result is by RQ4 cluster:

Game Cluster AI-assistant share of platform switches
Best Buds 0 — "list-browsers" (n=14) 2%
Best Buds 1 — "AI-assisted" (n=7) 33%
Townscaper 0 — typical (n=17) 2%
Townscaper 1 — "AI-quick" (n=4) 60%

This wasn't built into the clustering (RQ4 used only View AI response/ View info box action proportions) — it's an independent confirmation that the "AI-assisted"/"AI-quick" cluster names describe something real: those participants' platform switches concretely go to ChatGPT, Google AI Mode, and Meta.AI, not just to a same-named action category.

7.2 The AI-cluster writes longer queries — direction holds, but underpowered

Per-participant median query length (tokens), aggregated by RQ4 cluster (median rather than mean, and one query per participant rather than one row per query, to avoid pseudo-replication — an instance-level test looked dramatically "significant" purely from treating each of one person's many queries as an independent observation):

Game Cluster Median query length (tokens) Mann-Whitney p
Best Buds list-browsers 5.25
Best Buds AI-assisted 13.0 0.13
Townscaper typical 4.0
Townscaper AI-quick 14.5 0.13

A real, substantial, consistently-directional effect (2.5–3.6× longer median queries) — makes mechanistic sense, since AI assistants invite full-sentence prompts where search engines invite keywords — but at proper participant-level n (7 vs. 14; 4 vs. 17) it doesn't clear conventional significance. One participant (ID15) is a striking illustration: in the AI-assisted/AI-quick cluster in both games, with individual queries running to 239 and 189 tokens — paragraph-length prompts, not search terms. The cluster-level effect holds even excluding that one participant (Best Buds AI-cluster median 9.75 vs. 5.25 tokens without them), so it isn't purely an ID15 artifact.

Query length does not change across a Best Buds session (first-half vs. second-half mean tokens, Wilcoxon p=0.43) — RQ3 §3.3's "entropy rises through the session" finding is about broadening which actions happen, not writing longer queries as the session wears on.

7.3 Townscaper's played-second self-loops are mostly re-checking the same source

The strongest RQ6.4 finding was View single result's 47% self-loop rate in Townscaper when played after Best Buds (vs. 4% when played first, §6.4). The new source data specifies what that self-loop actually is:

Game Self-loops Same source repeated
Best Buds 10 30%
Townscaper 17 65%

Nearly two-thirds of Townscaper View single result → View single result transitions revisit the same site rather than checking a different one. (Almost all of these 17 self-loops come from played-second sessions — only 1 occurred in a played-first session, too sparse to compare rates by order directly — but that near-total concentration in played-second sessions is itself consistent with §6.4's story.) This sharpens "hesitancy/double-checking" from §6.4 into something more literal: re-opening the same Steam page or Reddit thread repeatedly, not sampling a wider set of sources before deciding.

↑ Back to top

8. RQ8 — Which platforms are involved in finding Townscaper, and in what order?

Follow-up to RQ7, requested by the researcher: not just where platform switches go pooled across a session, but which platforms are actually involved in finding Townscaper specifically, which one is typically showing when the game gets identified, and whether there's a consistent order. Best Buds is included throughout as a cheap comparison column. Full outputs in results/rq8_platform_sequence/; code: analysis/rq8_platform_sequence.py.

8.1 Search engines are the hub; everything else is a spoke

Categorizing every Platform switch destination in Townscaper sessions (n=63): search engines account for 78% (Google/DuckDuckGo variants), storefronts (Steam) 8%, AI assistants and community sites (Reddit) 6% each. Best Buds looks almost identical in proportion (78% search engine) but leans harder on AI assistants (10% vs. Townscaper's 6%) — consistent with RQ7 §7.1's cluster-level finding, just visible here in the raw game-level totals too.

The order is the more interesting part:

From \ To Search engine AI assistant Storefront Community
Search engine 26 1 5 3
Storefront 3 1 0 0
Community 2 0 0 0

Storefronts and community sites only ever connect back to a search engine — never to each other directly, and search engine is by far the most common state to switch into from anywhere. That's a hub-and-spoke pattern: search engines are the hub participants keep returning to; Steam/Reddit/etc. are spokes visited and left, not a chain (e.g. never Steam → Reddit directly).

Best Buds shows the identical structure, just with more AI-assistant traffic through the hub — the shape of platform navigation, like the action-level backbone in RQ2, doesn't depend on which game or whether it gets solved.

This also shows up as where sessions open and close: 85% of Townscaper sessions make their first platform switch to a search engine, and 80% end on the same category they started on (n=20 sessions with ≥1 switch). Best Buds opens on a search engine even more often (95%) but returns to the same category only 62% of the time, and is more likely to end on an AI assistant (29% vs. Townscaper's 20%) — a session that keeps wandering, matching RQ3/RQ4's picture of Best Buds as the less settled, more exploratory task.

8.2 Steam is where people look; the "aha" moment is scattered elsewhere

Steam is the single most-visited source when participants open a single result in Townscaper (23 of the ~89 View single result instances — by far the top individual site, ahead of Reddit at 5). But looking specifically at what's on screen right before the session actually ends (closing action = View single result, n=12 of 21 sessions — the plurality closing move, ahead of View info box at 4, View result list at 3, View AI response at 2): Steam accounts for only 2 of those 12. The rest are one-off — a gaming blog (videospielgeschichten.de, gamestar.de, Ratgeber-videospiele.dk), a community/wiki-style page (The Cozy Gaming Nook, Gamers-place), a video (TikTok video, Youtube), a Google Image result, or the game's own site directly.

So Steam functions as a browsing hub — a place to check candidates — much more than a confirming one. The moment someone actually recognizes the game tends to come from a smaller, more idiosyncratic source, not the platform they spent the most time on. (One caveat carried over from earlier sections: outcome isn't a ground-truth label here — ID9's Townscaper session, the one inferred non-solver from RQ3/RQ6.4, closes on View result list, not View single result, so it's correctly excluded from this "closing move" tally rather than contaminating it.)

↑ Back to top

10. RQ10 — Does a finer platform breakdown surface image-search reliance?

Researcher-provided data/platform_map.json splits RQ7/RQ8's coarse "Platform switch" destination categories (search engine / AI assistant / storefront / community) into finer ones — Web search, Image search, Conversational search, and Game search, plus Other for everything rare — motivated by an impression that participants relied heavily on image search specifically, which the coarser buckets couldn't distinguish from ordinary web search. Applied via a new context column (analysis/data.py) that reconstructs which platform/website each action happens on by forward-filling the most recent Platform switch destination within a session. Full methodology in docs/planning_and_background.md §4.9; code in analysis/rq10_finer_platform_categories.py; outputs in results/rq10_finer_platform_categories/.

10.1 Image search is the second most-used category overall

Category Count Share
Web search 502 46%
Image search 312 29%
Conversational search 128 12%
Game search 121 11%
Other 24 2%

The motivating impression holds up: image search is a clear second to web search, well ahead of conversational (AI-assistant) search, in both games — 240/823 events (29%) in Best Buds vs Bad Guys, 72/264 (27%) in Townscaper.

Both transition graphs use the same fixed 13-state layout (7 base actions plus 6 platform-switch categories that actually occur in the data), so a state's position is identical across the two games — comparable at a glance rather than needing to hunt for which circle moved. Platform switch: Image search behaves like a normal search hub in both: mostly followed by View result list (77–84%), occasionally by another Query.

10.2 Image-search reliance and AI-assistant reliance are separate styles

Cross-checked against RQ4's clusters (§4), since it turned out to be a striking result: in Townscaper, the 4-member "AI-quick" feature-cluster (ID6, ID7, ID15, ID18 — high View AI response share) uses image search 0% of the time, unanimously, while the 16-member majority cluster averages 35.2% (individual range 0–81%). Best Buds shows the same direction, more weakly: 15.4% vs. 29.7%. Read next to RQ4's original AI-vs-majority split, this suggests image-search reliance and AI-assistant reliance are two distinct, largely mutually exclusive search styles — leaning on an assistant to shortcut the search, or leaning on reverse image search to visually match the game — rather than something people mix.

Update: the two data-quality issues previously flagged here (a "Conservational search" typo, and "Moby Games"/"MobyGames" mapping inconsistently) are now fixed at the source in platform_map.json, which the researcher also simplified — every rare category (video, news, list, product, forum search, TikTok, etc.) is now folded into one Other bucket, leaving the five categories in §10.1's table. An earlier version of this section also used the wrong denominator for the overall shares above (all rows with a resolved context, rather than the subset actually eligible for categorization); both the table and the image-search shares here now reflect the corrected 1,087-event base — the by-cluster comparison below was already computed correctly and is unchanged.

11. RQ11 — Search tactics as recurring action sub-sequences

Researcher-proposed, inspired by Wildemuth, Oh & Marchionini (2010), who derived named search "tactics" from Maximal Repeating Patterns (MRP) in coded action sequences, then manually discarded any MRP occurrence subsumed by (contained within) a longer one before grouping the survivors by hand. Two automated, complementary takes on that idea, run per game on the coded action sequences (Experiment ended excluded — a fixed bookkeeping marker, not a search move). Full methodology in docs/planning_and_background.md §4.8; code in analysis/rq11_maximal_repeats.py; outputs in results/rq11_maximal_repeats/.

11.1 The flat view: supermaximal repeats

A supermaximal repeat is a maximal repeated sub-sequence with no single occurrence contained inside an occurrence of another, longer repeat — found via a suffix array and LCP array, and verified against a brute-force reference implementation. That occurrence-level containment check is the automated equivalent of Wildemuth's manual dedup step.

How to read the figure below. Each strip is one recurring tactic; each colored box is one step, left to right, colored by action (same palette as RQ2). The number after each strip is how many distinct participants used that exact tactic at least once — not the raw count of occurrences, which can overstate things if one participant repeats a tactic within their own session (see the callout below the figure for a concrete case). A tactic is only reported here once it clears length ≥3 (bigrams are already covered by RQ2's n-gram tables) and is used by ≥3 distinct participants — a much lower bar than Wildemuth's count-≥5 on 141 sequences, since this dataset has only 13–21 sequences per game. Every tactic that clears the bar in this data happens to be used by exactly 3 participants — nothing reaches 4 or more — so there's no frequency variation left to rank by; rows are then ordered by length, longest first, which is why the strips read top-to-bottom as "longest first" rather than "most common first."

Best Buds vs Bad Guys (unsolved, 0/21) has 143 supermaximal repeats overall, of which 9 clear the bar (longest: 7 steps); Townscaper (solved, 20/21) has 48 overall, but none reach 3 participants — its best candidate, a 4-step check-and-move-on pattern, is used by only 2.

Since the strips alone don't make it obvious which short steps recur across several of the 9 tactics, here's that directly: for each 2-step sub-pattern, in how many of the 9 tactics it appears at least once (counted once per tactic, not per raw occurrence):

Building block In how many of the 9 tactics
Query → View result list 7
View result list → Query 6
Platform switch → Query 4
Platform switch → View result list 4
View result list → Platform switch 3
View single result → View result list 3
View result list → View single result 3

Query ↔ View result list — the core loop from RQ2 §2.1 — is the backbone of nearly every tactic here; what makes a tactic rather than just that loop is which detour (Platform switch or View single result) gets threaded through it, and in what order.

Townscaper produces no report-worthy flat tactics at all — a second, independent confirmation (after §11.2 below) that its sessions don't develop recurring multi-step habits the way Best Buds' do.

11.2 The hierarchical view: a RE-PAIR grammar

The flat list above can't show a repeated pattern that's itself built out of a smaller repeated pattern, and (as just shown) can undercount badly if a "repeat" is really one participant looping within their own session. A RE-PAIR grammar (Larsson & Moffat, 1999 — a Sequitur-family algorithm, chosen over implementing Sequitur directly since its offline "replace the most frequent adjacent pair, then repeat" loop is much easier to verify correctly at this scale than Sequitur's cascading online bookkeeping) fixes both: every rule has exactly two symbols on its right-hand side, so a rule referencing another rule is a tactic built from smaller tactics, and every node — not just the whole tree — gets its own participant count.

How to read the figure below. Each panel is one RE-PAIR rule, picked as one of the 5 most composite (longest fully-expanded) rules for that game, regardless of how many participants use it — this set is not filtered the way §11.1's tactics are, so it can and does surface rarer, longer structures. Colored circles are terminal actions (leaf of the tree); grey circles are sub-rules, each labeled with how many distinct participants have that exact sub-pattern somewhere in their session. The panel title gives the whole rule's participant count and length; every other grey circle in the tree is a smaller "sub-tactic" in its own right, with its own, usually much higher, participant count.

Reading R42 (leftmost, 2 participants, 12 steps): its right child decomposes down through a sub-rule that is Query → View result list repeated twice — that specific 4-step doubled loop alone is used by 11 participants, over half the game, even though the full 12-step R42 it sits inside is used by only 2. That's the point of annotating every node: Query → View result list itself (the smallest sub-rule visible, bottom of several branches) is used by all 21 participants — near-universal — so what's actually rare about R42 isn't any of its pieces, it's this specific 12-step chaining of very common pieces.

The clearest single example of the occurrence-vs-participant gap from §11.1 shows up in the second panel, R41 (1 participant, 10 steps): raw occurrence count is 2, but both occurrences belong to the same participant, ID4, who performed this exact 10-step Platform switch/Query/View result list sequence twice in a row (27 actions apart) within their own Best Buds session — a genuine stuck-in-a-loop moment, not a tactic shared across participants at all.

Townscaper's top-5 most composite rules max out at 2 participants each — the same ceiling §11.1's flat view found, now confirmed by a completely independent method starting from the opposite end (longest structures first, rather than most-shared first). Its trees are also shallower: mostly one level of nesting (a Platform switch → Query or Query → View result list pair, occasionally paired with itself once more) rather than Best Buds' multi-level chains.

This is a third, independent line pointing at the same conclusion as RQ3's plateau finding (§3.3) and RQ4's clustering: Best Buds sessions loop and backtrack in ways Townscaper sessions mostly don't — not just more often, but more compositionally, with small, very common loops getting chained into longer, much rarer ones rather than the session just ending.

↑ Back to top

12. RQ12 — Tactics with Platform switch split by finer category

Direct extension of RQ11, reusing its exact machinery (supermaximal repeats + RE-PAIR grammar, participant-count-based reporting) but with the Platform switch state itself expanded into its data/platform_map.json category wherever known — Platform switch: Web search, : Image search, etc. — the same convention RQ9 used for the Markov models. Only the Platform switch symbol changes; Query, View result list, and every other action stay as they are, unlike RQ10's broader context-based recoloring — this keeps RQ12 a direct, comparable variant of RQ11 rather than a different question. Motivated by RQ11's building-blocks table (§11.1), where generic Platform switch steps thread through most of Best Buds' reported tactics: were those genuinely shared tactics, or different participants' different platform choices collapsing to the same coarse label? Full methodology in docs/planning_and_background.md §4.10; code in analysis/rq12_platform_tactics.py; outputs in results/rq12_platform_tactics/.

Both true and false. Best Buds' tactic count does drop once the platform is visible (9 → 7 reported tactics vs. RQ11) — some of RQ11's coarse-label matches really were different participants making different platform choices. But it isn't a full collapse:

3 of the 7 survivors still name a specific platform and still clear the ≥3-participant bar — Platform switch: Conversational search once, Platform switch: Image search twice, Platform switch: Web search once. Switching to image search specifically (not just "switching platforms" in general) is itself a tactic several participants converge on independently — a sharper version of RQ10's image-search-reliance finding, now visible at the multi-step tactic level rather than just the raw category count.

The RE-PAIR tree surfaces a genuinely new composite RQ11 couldn't show: rule R34 (3 participants, 8 steps) chains a web-search detour into an image-search detour within one recurring tactic — Platform switch: Web search → Query → Platform switch: Image search → View result list → Query → View result list → Query → View result list. Reading the nesting: the Platform switch: Image search → View result list pair alone (rule R3) is used by 14 participants — two-thirds of the game — even though the full 8-step tactic it sits inside is used by only 3; the innermost Query → View result list loop (rule R1) is used by all 21, same as in RQ11. The rarity is still in the specific chaining, not the pieces.

Townscaper goes the other way: RQ11 had zero qualifying tactics, RQ12 has one — Query → View AI response → View single result, no platform switch involved at all. It wasn't visible in RQ11 because a longer, platform-switch-involving pattern used to subsume its occurrences (§11.1's subsumption step); splitting the alphabet broke that containment and let the shorter pattern surface on its own. Worth keeping in mind for any future granularity change: a finer alphabet doesn't only fragment tactics, it can also un-bury shorter ones a coarser alphabet's subsumption step had been hiding.

↑ Back to top

13. RQ13 — Does prior chatbot experience explain the AI-cluster?

Researcher-provided pre-experiment questionnaire data (data/survey_data/) adds, among other things, self-rated familiarity (0–4) with six kinds of search system, rated independently rather than as one scale. Chatbot-style AI tools is the one item with real variance (0–4, unlike e.g. General web search engines, which is 3–4 for nearly everyone) and a direct line to RQ4's clustering: does the "AI-assisted"/"AI-quick" cluster (§4) actually consist of people who came in more experienced with chatbot tools, or is the cluster purely a behavioral pattern with no prior-experience signature? Code in analysis/rq13_experience.py; outputs in results/rq13_experience/.

Yes, clearly, in both games:

Game Majority-cluster median AI-cluster median Mann-Whitney p
Best Buds vs Bad Guys 0.5 4.0 0.002
Townscaper 1.0 3.5 0.036

Best Buds' "AI-assisted" cluster (n=7) has a median self-rated chatbot familiarity of 4 out of 4 — the ceiling — against 0.5 for the rest of the sample (n=14); Townscaper's "AI-quick" cluster (n=4) shows the same pattern at smaller n. Both comparisons are significant despite the small group sizes, which is itself informative about the size of the effect.

This is a different kind of validation than RQ7 §7.1's platform-switch destinations or RQ10 §10.2's image-search cross-check: those confirmed the cluster's behavior was internally consistent with its name, using data from the same sessions being clustered. This one reaches outside the session entirely, to a questionnaire answered before either game was played. The AI-cluster isn't just a behavioral pattern that happens to look AI-heavy in hindsight — the people in it already knew their way around chatbot tools going in, and that prior familiarity is exactly where they turned once the task got hard.

↑ Back to top

14. Discussion

Seven RQs, read separately, are seven answers. Read together, they converge on a smaller number of claims about what a post-play game search actually is. This section pulls those threads together, relates them to the literature framing in docs/planning_and_background.md §3, and states plainly what would and wouldn't survive a larger sample.

14.1 One search grammar, one game-specific ending

The single clearest result across RQ2, RQ3, and RQ6.4 is that the process and the outcome are separable. RQ2 found a tight, near-universal loop — Query → View result list, splitting into reformulate / drill in / switch platform — that RQ3 then showed is statistically indistinguishable between a game nobody solves and a game almost everyone solves (§3.1: 5 of 7 states, p ≥ 0.12). The two games don't diverge in how people search. They diverge in exactly one place: what happens after View single result, i.e. whether looking closely at a candidate result turns into a closing move or not (§2.2, §3.1). RQ6.4 then found that even this divergence is order-sensitive — the same state (View single result) that separates the games also separates played-first from played-second Townscaper sessions, with the same signature (branch out and conclude vs. loop back on the same source, §6.4, §7.3).

This is a more specific claim than the classic stage models (Kuhlthau 1991; Marchionini 1995 — planning doc §3.1) would predict on their own. Those models describe search as a sequence of qualitatively different phases building toward resolution; what we see here is closer to a single stable phase (the query/browse loop) that either does or doesn't hand off to a terminal phase, with the handoff — not the exploration — being where task and prior experience leave their mark. It also sharpens Xie & Joo (2010, planning doc §3.2)'s Markov-transition approach: where they found a broader tactic space across heterogeneous web-search tasks, our narrowly-scoped, closed-vocabulary task collapses to a backbone simple enough that where it diverges is itself the finding, not just that it diverges. RQ8's platform-level view (§8.1) shows the same hub-and-spoke shape underneath the action-level loop — search engines as the hub, storefronts/communities/AI assistants as spokes returned from, never chained directly to each other — in both games, regardless of outcome. The grammar RQ2 describes at the action level and the grammar RQ8 describes at the platform level are the same grammar, described twice.

14.2 A personal search style, orthogonal to whether the task succeeds

RQ4 found a consistent subgroup in both games (Best Buds n=7, Townscaper n=4, overlapping — §4.3, ARI=0.47) defined by reliance on View AI response/View info box rather than View result list. RQ7 then grounded that split in something the clustering never saw: those participants' platform switches concretely go to ChatGPT, Google AI Mode, and Meta.AI (33–60% vs. 2%, §7.1), and their queries run 2.5–3.6× longer median tokens (§7.2) — full prompts, not keywords. Put together with §4.3's cross-game persistence, this looks like a genuine individual disposition — how someone chooses to interrogate a search system — that sits orthogonal to the resolved/unresolved split from RQ3: it shows up in the game nobody solves and the game almost everyone solves alike, and doesn't move the needle on whether Best Buds gets solved (nobody in either cluster solves it). This is the one finding in this study without a close antecedent in the cited literature (planning doc §3.2, which predates conversational AI search as a "platform" alongside search engines and stores) — search-tactic transition studies from the 2000s/2010s (Goodrum et al. 2003; Jansen et al. 2007) had no AI-assistant state to find a cluster around.

14.3 Prior experience leaves a targeted mark, not a diffuse one

RQ6 asked the researcher's order question broadly and found nothing at the level of aggregate session features (§6.1: all p ≥ 0.24) — order doesn't make people query more, switch platforms more, or take longer. RQ6.4 then asked the sharper version and found two specific, well-supported effects hiding under that null: Townscaper's closing-move state behaves differently by order (§6.4, survives Bonferroni, strengthens after removing the opening-move confound), and Best Buds' second-half exploration only broadens significantly when Best Buds is played after a Townscaper win (§6.4, entropy p=0.032 vs. p=0.625). RQ6 §6.2's opening-carryover result (own-pair distance below chance, p=0.029, stronger after Best-Buds-first) is the same pattern one level up: prior experience doesn't rewrite the whole session, it recolors specific, identifiable junctures — how a session opens, and how it closes. That's a more precise and more falsifiable claim than "frustration/confidence carries over," and it's the reason RQ6.4 was worth doing as a follow-up to RQ6 rather than stopping at the null in §6.1.

14.4 What the measurement caveats change, and what they don't

RQ5's finding — annotators agree almost perfectly on labels (92–100% when aligned) but vary substantially on segmentation (annotator2's Townscaper coverage: 42%, §5.1) — matters for how the length- and count-based results above should be read. It's good news for RQ2–RQ4's transition and cluster analyses, which depend on relative ordering and type of actions, not on catching every micro-event. It's a real caveat for absolute session-length comparisons (RQ1 §1.3, RQ3 §3.2): the 5 participants annotator2 coded (ID6–ID10) are plausible undercounts relative to how the other annotators would have segmented the same recordings. None of RQ1–RQ8's conclusions hinge on any one of those 5 participants, so this doesn't overturn anything — but it's the reason this report keeps saying "treat as descriptive" rather than asserting population-level session-length values with false precision.

14.5 What a larger sample would (and wouldn't) buy

Three results are directional and plausible but didn't clear conventional significance at this N, and are worth naming together rather than re-litigating individually: the Best-Buds-first opening-carryover asymmetry (§6.2, p=0.077, n=10/11), the AI-cluster query-length difference (§7.2, p≈0.13, n=4–7 per cluster), and Townscaper's 3-cluster-vs-2 instability under a handful of added events (§4.2). All three share a cause, not just a symptom: an already-small study (N=21) sliced further by order or by cluster leaves single-digit cells. None of them are artifacts — all three point the same direction as their better-powered siblings (RQ6.4's Townscaper closing-move effect, RQ4's Best Buds AI-cluster split, RQ7 §7.1's platform-category confirmation) — but a replication with a larger or unbalanced-by-design sample (e.g. deliberately oversampling one play order) is what would turn "suggestive" into "confirmed" for these three specifically. The core-loop/closing-move distinction (§14.1) and the annotator-segmentation gap (§14.4), by contrast, are both well-powered as reported and unlikely to move with more data of the same kind.
